1. Präteritum in writing, Perfekt in speech

In spoken German, especially in the south, people use almost only the Perfekt (ich bin gegangen). In written texts — novels, articles, memoirs, fairy tales — the narrative tense is the Präteritum (ich ging). Spoken exceptions: sein, haben, the modal verbs and a few others (war, hatte, konnte, gab es).
I went down to the cellar. The light went out. (spoken)
I went down to the cellar. The light went out. (written)
to penetrate, to force your way
Watch out for pairs that are easy to confuse: bitten – bat (to ask) / beten – betete (to pray) / bieten – bot (to offer).
3. The second person in the Präteritum
These forms appear mainly in letters, poems and literary dialogues: “Du kamst immer zu spät, aber du kamst.” In speech you say “Du bist immer zu spät gekommen”.
Writers alternate very short sentences with long ones. Short sentences create tension: “Das Licht erlosch. Die Wände zitterten. Meine Mutter schwieg.” Long sentences describe and explain.

In January two thousand and thirty-six, Grete decided to write down her memories. More precisely, she decided to have someone write them down for her, because by now her hands shook so badly that she could barely hold a cup, let alone a pen. She had hesitated for a long time. “Who would want to read an old woman's stories?” she had said to Ludwig when he visited her at the care home at Christmas, with a copy of his book, which by now was in its third print run. Ludwig had just pointed at the book. “That's what they said about an old tram driver's stories too,” he had replied. “And now Mrs Winter is printing it for the third time.”

Grete had said nothing. But two days later Mrs Petersen rang Lena and asked whether “the girl with the metronome” could perhaps stay an hour longer on Wednesdays. Mrs Hoffmann had something in mind, she said, and wouldn't say what. Lena asked Elif, Elif asked her mother, and Ayşe Yilmaz, who also had piano lessons with Grete every Wednesday and knew what it meant when Grete “had something in mind”, said yes at once. That same evening Ludwig mentioned it to Mrs Winter on the phone, just in passing. Mrs Winter was silent for a moment. Then she said: “Mr Brandt, when these memoirs are finished, I want to be the first to read them. Promise me.” Ludwig promised. He didn't know yet that by doing so he had brought a second book into the world, and that it would not be his.

And so it came about that from the second Wednesday in January, Elif no longer went to the care home just for her piano lesson but stayed on for an hour afterwards, with a thick exercise book and a fountain pen Ludwig had given her, the same old fountain pen with which he had signed Mara's marriage certificate as a witness. Grete sat in bed or, on good days, in the armchair by the window, with a blanket on her knees, and dictated. She dictated slowly, with her eyes closed, and sometimes she was silent for whole minutes, until Elif thought she had fallen asleep. But she never fell asleep. She was only looking for the right word. And when she found it, she opened her eyes and said it, clearly, syllable by syllable, like a teacher giving a dictation.

At first there was an argument. Not about the content, but about the tense. Elif had learned at school that you use the Präteritum in compositions, but at home she spoke, like almost everyone in Berlin, in the Perfekt, and when Grete told her stories, she told them in the Perfekt too, like anyone remembering something. “Ich bin in den Keller gegangen,” Grete dictated. “Ich ging in den Keller,” Elif wrote. Grete didn't notice at once. Only when Elif read the first page back to her did she raise her hand. “That doesn't sound like me,” she said. “It sounds like a book.” “It is a book,” said Elif. Grete was silent for a long time. Then she smiled. “You're right,” she said. “Keep writing. Like a book.”

And so, week by week, page by page, a story came into being that nobody on Kastanienallee had known in full, not even Ludwig. It began in February nineteen forty-four, in a block of flats in Wedding, on a night when the sirens howled at eleven o'clock and Grete's mother tore her out of bed, wrapped her in a coat and carried her down the stairs in her arms, four floors, to the cellar. Grete was seven. Her father had been at the front for two years, somewhere in the east, and wrote letters that grew shorter and shorter. In the cellar thirty people sat on wooden benches, women, children, old people, and a single light bulb hung from the ceiling and swung back and forth when the bombs fell in the distance.

“Then they came closer,” Grete dictated, and Elif wrote: “Then they came closer. The walls trembled. Plaster fell from the ceiling, fine as flour. The light went out. In the dark a child screamed, then a second, then all of them. My mother held me tight against her and was silent. She was silent all night. I could only hear her heart, which was beating faster than mine.” Elif stopped writing and looked at Grete. Grete's eyes were closed, and her hands lay still on the blanket, completely still, for the first time in weeks, as if the memory had driven the trembling away.

In the corner of the cellar there was an old piano. Nobody knew whose it was. It had been there since the house was built, so the neighbours said, too heavy to carry up the stairs, too out of tune to sell. The children sometimes played on it when there was no air raid, and it sounded like a cat whose tail you had trodden on. But that night, when all the children were screaming and the light had gone out, suddenly there was the sound of a match. A small flame glided through the darkness towards the piano, and in its light Grete saw an old man she knew: Mr Wendland from the third floor, who had once taught at the music school and no longer did, for reasons the adults only whispered about, and who since the previous autumn had been secretly giving her piano lessons in his flat, for a piece of bread an hour.

Mr Wendland put the candle on the piano, sat down and began to play. He didn't play a children's song. He played something slow and calm that Grete didn't know and that later, many years later, she recognised as Brahms, the Intermezzo in A major, opus 118. The piano was out of tune and some keys stuck, but he played anyway, and he played as if he weren't in a cellar in Wedding but in a concert hall. And one after another, the children stopped screaming. First the youngest. Then the others. In the end the cellar was so quiet that between the explosions you could hear only the piano and the flickering of the candle. “He played,” Grete dictated, “until the children stopped screaming. And then he played on, until the adults stopped crying.”

Elif wrote the sentence, slowly, with the old fountain pen, and didn't underline it, because in a book you don't underline anything. Then she asked what she had long wanted to ask: “Was it the metronome? The metronome you gave me?” Grete opened her eyes. “The metronome came later,” she said. “After the war. Mr Wendland went on giving me lessons, for free, for three years, in his flat, which was half destroyed. He didn't have a piano any more. All he had left was the metronome. I practised on the table. I drew the keys on the wood, in chalk. For three years I played the piano on a table.” She laughed softly. “You don't write that in the Perfekt, do you hear? You write that properly.”

That evening, when Elif came home, she didn't go straight to the piano as usual, the piano her family had had for two years, thanks to Katrin Krüger's article and a generous piano dealer. Instead she took a piece of chalk out of her school bag and, to her mother's great horror, drew a keyboard on the kitchen table, two octaves, with black and white keys, as accurately as she could. Then she sat down in front of it, closed her eyes and played the piece she was learning with Grete at the moment, a little waltz by Chopin, on the wood, without a single sound. Her mother stood in the doorway and wanted to tell her off. But then she saw her daughter's face and said nothing. Elif played to the end. When she opened her eyes, she just said: “You really can hear it. If you know it, you hear it.” The chalk stayed on the table for three days. Nobody wiped it off.

Elif wrote: “After the war Mr Wendland went on giving me lessons, for free, for three years, in his half-destroyed flat. He no longer had a piano, only a metronome. I drew the keys in chalk on the kitchen table and practised on it, every day, until my fingers heard the notes the wood couldn't play.” She read it to Grete. Grete listened, nodded and then said something Elif would never forget for the rest of her life: “It's better than the way I said it. You've made it more beautiful than it was. But not less true.” And at that moment Elif understood what Katrin Krüger had meant when she said that writing is not the same as telling. It is telling, combed until it shines.

One Wednesday at the end of February, when the first snow in weeks was falling outside, Ludwig came too. He sat quietly in the corner of the room, on the visitor's chair, and listened as Grete told of her first concert, at the Konzerthaus, in nineteen fifty-six, at the age of twenty, in a dress her mother had sewn from an old curtain. And how in the third row there sat an old man, very thin, with white hair, who didn't clap after the concert but just stood up, bowed and left. “I ran after him,” Grete dictated. “I ran in my curtain dress through the foyer and down the stairs and into the street. But he had disappeared. I never saw him again. Three months later I learned that Mr Wendland had died, a week after my concert.”

It was very quiet in the room. Outside, the snow was falling on the trees in the care home's garden. Ludwig cleared his throat. “And the metronome?” he asked softly. “How did it come to you?” Grete looked at the window. “His niece brought it to me,” she said. “In a shoebox. With a note. On it, in his handwriting, there was just one sentence.” She fell silent again. Elif was holding the pen above the paper, not breathing. “What did it say?” she asked at last, very quietly. Grete closed her eyes. “It said: «For the girl who played on the table. You heard it. I know.»” Elif wrote the sentence. Then she put the pen down, because now it was her hand that was shaking. Ludwig stood up, went over to Grete and took her hand, and for a long time nobody said anything, and none of them was ashamed of it. Outside it went on snowing, softly, as if even the snow didn't want to disturb them.
